messages.content: Write an internal post arguing for blameless postmortems at a company that does not do them yet. Around 250 words.

Here's the draft:

---

**We should stop asking who broke it**

Last month's checkout outage took 4 hours to resolve. The write-up took three weeks, and I'd bet most of you never read it. That's not because nobody cared. It's because the review turned into a question about whose commit it was, and once that happens the person who knows the most about what went wrong is also the person with the most reason to stay quiet.

I want us to run postmortems the way Google, Etsy, and Stripe do: blameless. No names attached to causes. The write-up asks what the system allowed, not who did it.

The argument isn't kindness. It's data quality. An engineer who fears the review will write the shortest defensible account of the incident. An engineer who doesn't will tell you that the deploy dashboard had been showing stale data for six weeks and everyone had quietly learned to ignore it. That second thing is the actual bug. You only ever hear about it from someone who feels safe saying it out loud.

The usual objection is that removing blame removes accountability. It doesn't. Accountability moves from the individual to the fix: every postmortem produces owned action items with dates, and we track completion. Missing those is a real performance conversation. Having caused an incident is not.

Concretely, I'm proposing we try this for one quarter. Any incident over 30 minutes gets a blameless write-up, published company-wide within five business days, using a template I'll draft this week.

Who's in?

---

248 words. Two things you may want to adjust before posting: swap the checkout outage for whatever incident your readers actually remember, and put a real name on the template owner if it isn't you.
Rewrite the text above. Keep the same length and the same purpose. Return only the rewritten text.

output:
**Stop asking whose commit it was**

The checkout outage in August ran four hours. The write-up landed three weeks later, and I doubt twenty people opened it. That isn't apathy. The review turned into an argument about attribution, and once that happens, the person who understands the failure best has every reason to say as little as possible.

So: blameless postmortems, the kind Google, Etsy, and Stripe have run for a decade. No names attached to causes. The document asks what the system permitted, not who typed the command.

The case for this isn't kindness. It's accuracy. Someone who expects to be judged writes the shortest account he or she can defend. Someone who doesn't will tell you the deploy dashboard had been serving stale data for six weeks and the team had quietly stopped trusting it. That's the real failure. You hear it only from a person who feels safe saying it out loud.

I know the objection. Drop blame, drop accountability. Wrong target. Accountability moves from the person to the repair: every postmortem ends with owned action items and dates, and we track whether they close. Blowing a deadline on one of those is a performance conversation. Being on shift when something broke is not.

Concretely, I want one quarter as a trial. Any incident over 30 minutes gets a blameless write-up, published company-wide within five business days, on a template I'll have ready this week.

Who wants in?
